items.title: Schuller Gunther — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: One of the greatest, maybe the greatest improvisation – it’s hard to say something is the greatest – is the solo that he played in All About Rosie of George Russell, because that is so perfect and great a solo that I really can’t think of anything that was so spontaneously created. There’s Art Tatum

ctx.x: Can you give us one of those?

Okay. I thought you’d never ask. I should tell you about two. One of them, I was able to have no influence, but the other one – I don’t make any big claims about this, that I caused them to be the great musicians they are. No, no, nothing. They were great musicians and phenomenal players whom I admired and adored and considered great geniuses in what they already did. The one interesting case: this was Bill Evans. As soon as Bill Evans came to New York – I can’t keep it all straight any more. It’s too far back,…

and Eric Dolphy, all of that was in the direction of atonality. John Lewis could not improvise atonally. He stayed in – beautifully – in tonal music. So Bill became one of my major resources, along with Richard Davis and people like that, and Scott LaFaro, who were into the more modern directions. I knew, and we all knew, that Bill was very heavily on drugs. Two things happened.
